Chapter Two: Understanding Why We React the Way We Do
Have you ever wondered why some situations just set you off, while others barely make a dent? There’s always something deeper going on beneath those strong reactions—a whole web of old habits, beliefs, and maybe even some fears you haven’t really looked at. Most of us pick these patterns up as kids, from our culture, or through past experiences. They run so deep, it’s easy to mistake them for who we really are.
Picture this: someone feels slighted every time they’re left out of group plans. It’s the same old story, right? “I’m not valued,” or “They don’t care about me.” And even though the pain is real, the reaction is shaped by years and years of similar moments. The mind just grabs onto these stories, replaying them every time something triggers that old wound.
I remember a friend telling me how, as a child, he was always left out of family decisions. Fast forward to adulthood, and he’d get waves of anger and hurt at work if he felt excluded—even if it was just a small thing. He knew his reaction didn’t quite fit the situation, but those feelings...they were tough to shake. It turned out the present moment was all tangled up with old pain.
That’s how the hook works—it latches onto those unresolved hurts and uses them to fuel anger or resentment. The mind convinces us that the only way to stay safe is to defend, attack, or just pull away. Most people never realize these reactions aren’t set in stone—they’re learned. And the good news? They can be understood, questioned, and even changed.
At the heart of this urge to react are two big drivers: attachment and aversion. Attachment is all about wanting to hang onto what feels good or familiar. Aversion? That’s our urge to push away anything threatening or uncomfortable. These two forces shape almost every emotional reaction we have—from the smallest annoyances to the biggest blowups.
Think about a parent who gets angry when their child won’t listen. Underneath that anger, there’s often a longing for respect, a sense of control, or maybe just a little peace and quiet. When those needs aren’t met, frustration builds. You’ll see the same pattern everywhere: a partner feeling ignored, a worker feeling unappreciated, a friend feeling betrayed.
Most of us try to deal with these feelings by blaming someone else or trying to fix the situation. But here’s something worth paying attention to—the real shift happens when we look inward and ask ourselves, “What am I hanging onto here? What am I trying so hard to avoid?” That kind of honest reflection takes real courage. It means facing some tough truths and maybe letting go of stories that no longer serve us.
One evening, a group of friends got together to talk about their struggles with anger. Everyone had a story—being criticized by a partner, dealing with a boss’s demands, or even just a rude stranger. As they listened to each other, they realized the details weren’t what mattered most. Underneath it all, they were caught in the same cycle of attachment and aversion, each one trying to guard themselves from pain.
And then, a simple but powerful insight started to emerge: emotions aren’t enemies to be fought—they’re messengers to be understood. When you really sit with your anger, resentment, or fear, you start to see what’s at the root of your reaction. That’s when a little space opens up—a space for compassion, not just for yourself, but for others who are also struggling.
Over time, those old habits start to lose their grip. Your mind gets less reactive, and your heart opens up just a bit more. The goal isn’t to never feel anger or pain again—it’s about learning to respond with awareness and kindness. Every moment of understanding brings a little more freedom, a little more peace.
